https://rajan-thakur.github.io/iphs400-mp2-cms/\r\n    56\t\r\n    57\t## Generative AI Use Statement\r\n    58\t\r\n    59\tThis project has been created entirely using the Claude Code tool, specifically the Sonnet 5 model with Medium, High and Extra effort for thinking, and later Opus 5.5 High. Medium/High thinking effort was used from the start of the project up to the creation of the spec. Creating tickets and implementing them was all done using Sonnet 5 Extra effort. Then, at /code-review, I switched to the Opus 5.5 model with High thinking effort. Switching to have more capable models was a decision influenced by a discussion with Professor Chun that the token usage rates at Sonnet 5 Medium effort are very low, so bumping up the model's capability to be at High or Extra or just switching to Opus 5.5 High while compacting the context once it gets filled up to about 40% is only advantageous. Opus 5.5 High does burn tokens a lot, but it was essential in /code-review.\r\n    60\t\r\n    61\tThe skills used for this project are the Matt Pocock skills /grill-with-docs, /to-spec, /to-tickets, /implement, /tdd, /code-review. The model followed these skills well at every thinking effort: it generated a spec and also handled a project trajectory pivot well when I presented it a pivot from the original idea that would align better with the rubric and the project's requirements.\r\n    62\t\r\n    63\tOne prompt I gave the model, answering its questions and clarifying my previous answers during the /grill-with-docs skill running: \"Q1 - Sorry yes, use that template on the github repo. Use the git commands to get that template. Q2 - Yes, make it me and faculty advisor are admin and editor is for officers. Admin - editor permissions + publish/unpublish + manage users. Editor - edit and create content. Q3 - Outlined in Q2. Q4 - Advisor is Doctor Diane Kahle, use placeholders for student officer names for now. Look up CSHS details on upper arlington high school. GPA req is 3.5 or above. Q5 - Add posts, pages and events and roster. Events and roster will be extra credit. Posts - dated, feed-like, announcements, meetings, events, pages - about/eligibility, events, roster, join, eligibility.\"\r\n    64\t* Here I was answering its clarifying questions on how the project should look like. This is before pivoting from the idea of a client-specific CMS to a general CMS and a client-specific website built on top of it. The model correctly asked me about things that I was (intentionally) vague about, which allowed me to make things specific.\r\n    65\t\r\n    66\tSecond prompt I gave the model (during the pivot): \"Hey, change of plans. We're building a CMS with no client in mind. I know the current grading rubric says we need a specific client, but we're pivoting now because professor updated it. Essentially, the goal is to make a Wordpress-style CMS but not specific to any client.\"\r\n    67\t* I prompted the model this because initially I was steering it to develop a CMS with Admin/Editor roles specific to the organization I chose (the client, the Upper Arlington High School Computer Science Honor Society, UAHS CSHS). After a conversation with Professor Chun, I understood that the CMS should be general with no client specifically in mind, but then I need to use the CMS to create a custom website for a client. The model responded by actually asking questions about the implementation, which is good because it asked for clarifiation rather than guessing. I later clarified everything I meant in my prompt, saying that \"client specificity\" is still part of the project but only after the CMS is built separately.\r\n    68\t\r\n    69\tOne model failure occured during class, on the 1st of October. It wasn't a developmental failure, but rather a context management issue. This was in a different session from the one I had for this SWE Matt Pocock process. Since the context length fills up quickly in this SWE process, I prompted it to set up two hooks, where 1 hook warns me that Sonnet 5 is at 30% context fill, and the other runs /compact at 40%. As it turns out, it wasn't able to create the second hook and automatically run /compact at 40% context fill, so I told it to just change the hook just to block me out from sending messages. But then, Claude didn't check the context length limit for Sonnet 5 and just assumed it was 200k, which shut me out of my mini project session because the context length was already filled to 250k (approximately) tokens. To resolve this, I then had to manually go into the hooks in my global .claude folder and change the context window length to 1M because I couldn't prompt Claude to do so. Late I ended up just removing this second hook entirely, now relying only on the first \"warning\" hook so I compact the conversation, because the shut-off at 40% was inflexible.  \r\n    70\tAnother model failure I think is important to mention is the code it generated during the /implement phase. I switched to Opus 5.5 high at /code-review, and it flagged many bugs that it found in the project. It subsequently cleanly fixed them and successfully passed the code through a test suite, so this was more of an ephemeral and self-correcting issue, but I decided to mention it here anyway.\r\n    71\t\r\n    72\tNote for new Oct 15 (16th grace) deadline: I now switched to Opus 5.5 xhigh for all of my tasks. This was worthwhile because it flagged many issues against the new rubric that went unnoticed previously. The model chews up tokens quickly but handoff documents and /compact deal with this fine.\r\n    73\t\r\n    74\tAlso, an important clarification. After miscommunication with the model during one of the early planning stages during the grill session, the model proceeded to write a token usage plan as follows: first Sonnet 5 high/xhigh for the planning stages (/grill-with-docs, /to-spec, /to-tickets), then Sonnet 5 Medium for the implementation (/implement) and then Sonnet 5 high again for /code-review. That was not my original intention. I originally intended to use a different set of thinking efforts and models for the stages. But the model had already written this different plan into the token budget plan document. After implementation, I had noticed this discrepancy, and decided to clarify what the original plan was with commit 16c61f2.\r\n    75\t\r\n    76\t## Backends used\r\n    77\t\r\n    78\t| Backend | Model(s) |\r\n    79\t| ------- | -------- |\r\n    80\t| Anthropic | Sonnet 5 Medium, Sonnet 5 High, Sonnet 5 xHigh, Opus 5.5 High, Opus 5.5 xHigh |\r\n    81\t\r\n    82\tI only used Anthropic's models, specifically Sonnet 5 Medium, Sonnet 5 High, Sonnet 5 Extra High, Opus 5.5 High, Opus 5.5 xHigh. I used VS Code as my source code editor for this full project, with just a Windows command prompt open for Claude Code. I tried to set up and use Orca (agentic IDE), but I didn't find it as comfortable as VS Code.\r\n {"parentUuid":"7293a8b3-0896-410a-9e4e-414d1a4be51a","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"73092da2-53ea-49a2-8e10-93f9fbd5b5ef","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01Fd3HcvWaWoYLwtAkpck2Gc","type":"tool_result","content":"     1\t# Project Report\r\n     2\t\r\n     3\t* (a) What I built and which grill decisions were mine  \r\n     4\tTo build the CMS I used the AI only, and none of the code for the CMS is mine.\r\n     5\tOne major grill decision I made were to pivot away from a client-specific CMS to a general CMS with a separate client website built using the CMS. This was a major decision done in the early stage, which also led to me prompting it to change the already generated tech spec. This decision was influenced by new information about grading that I received verbally from Professor Chun about needing to create a general CMS with a website built on top of it, rather than a specific type of CMS.\r\n     6\tOther grill decisions I made were generally refinements of what the AI proposed, such as what Admin/Editor permissions should look like (such as that Editors should be able to delete content, I decided to add this because it can make using the CMS quicker instead of having to get admin permission each time, and anyone that edits a website should be trusted with the content) and what the CMS features should be. This is all verifiable with the transcripts and the CONTEXT.md file. The decision date for all this is 9185fe8 on the 1st of October.\r\n     7\tHowever, I built the custom, client-specific website for the Upper Arlington High School Computer Science Honor Society with client Dr. Diane Kahle in mind. I used the complete CMS to build it. I created two Posts on the \"/\" (main) page. One post is just a welcoming post, and the other is about an annual event that the CSHS chapter conducts, which is called Hour of Code. I created/expanded a computer science coursework page, the About page (which had everything from mission and why you should join to graduation awards) and also the Contact us page where I linked Dr. Diane Kahle's email. The website is live on GitHub pages. The commits were done to gh-pages and they are bce4dd6 and 5db2c46 (both on October 7th). Also, the title of the site is \"UAHS CSHS\", which just stands for Upper Arlington High School Computer Science Honor Society. I used the features that were built during the development phases of the CMS, and they worked correctly. The \"Hour of Code\" post was first written using the Editor account and then published using the admin account. I also used the revision history feature, specifically with 8 revisions and one roll back on the Contact Us page. The computer science coursework page had 3 revisions and the About page had 5 revisions. \r\n     8\t* (b) The AI didn't necessarily make stuff up but it did drift from what the rubric requested during the /implement stage, such as when it didn't take into account that a .env.example should work properly when the commands get fired off. This was to be expected, because the model was a Sonnet 5 at Extra thinking effort but not as capable as Opus 5.5 High. The workflow caught it here in the sense that when I ran /code-review, as detailed in the README.md file, I switched to Opus 5.5 High and it immediately spotted a bunch of issues. It then subsequently asked about these errors, I confirmed that it should go fix them, and it fixed all the bugs and ran tests that successfully passed. This was ticket 10 (T10, issue #11), and it was at line 18 in /app/settings.py that \"load_dotenv\" was added. So /code-review was useful to make sure that I wasn't proceeding to push any commits with hallucinated and incorrect code. This is verifiable with the transcript specifically, as it shows how I ran /code-review and that the model flagged all those bugs. This is all at the commits e043236 (most issues weres solved in this one), 3334e8e and e9dfb18 on the 6th of October.\r\n     9\t* (c) The skills I used were just the main workflow Matt Pocock skills, meaning /grill-with-docs, /to-spec, /to-tickets, /implement and /code-review. since those are the most applicable to this project. I used them because that's essentially the point of the project, and also, they make the AI SWE process very easy to go through because you can clarify what you want with the project and also steer the AI in a specific direction, and also it mitigates a lot of the issues of AI right now, such as context drift or hallucinations, etc. A prompt style I used a few times was telling the model to basically \"perform a gap analysis,\" which is where it compares the project against the rubric and manual and verifies if everything is correct or if I'm short on points. It is also useful because it lets me know exactly what the next steps should be to maximize points. A resource I used is the Claude Code documentation just to remind myself of what certain commands like /status and /context do. The pivot from a client-specific CMS to a general CMS with a client-specific website resulted in more planning time, but overall the idea was better aligned with what Professor Chun expects, which is why the switch was made.\r\n    10\t* (d) Future improvements include improving the design of the CMS so it looks prettier, and including more features such as themes and templates for website designs. These would be useful to add, both for convenience when using the CMS (nicer layout) and to be able to build websites with more features. Additionally, one very important feature to add is media uploads such as adding images. This would make the CMS more useful for the client, Dr. Diane Kahle, who could then add pictures of events such as hackathons and hour of code, which would help promote the chapter better. It would also be an improvement to add an events calendar, so that it is easy to keep track of the latest events. For now, the main page displays the latest posts, which is the only way to see the events.\r\n    11\t\r\n    12\tAdditionally, to explain the context threshold hook, it essentially keeps track of the context length with a percentage bar and the model being used, and at certain thresholds, it warns about the context length increasing, and then documents it by creating a row in the \"usage-ledger.csv\" file.\r\n    13\t\r\n    14\tAlso, I wanted to note a couple of things:\r\n    15\t* The /implement process was sort of done in one go rather than in separate sessions. There were ticket blocks, but it wasn't done one session per ticket.\r\n    16\t* There was also a Windows app alias issue, where when the hooks used to write new rows to the usage-ledger.csv file were activated, they called on python3 instead of python, and that didn't work for my system. Essentially there is a large gap that doesn't show the token usage during the implementation phase. \r\n    17\t\r\n    18\tWith that said, here's the comparison between the token budget plan and the usage ledger\r\n    19\t* The plan was to use about 20% on /grill-with-docs, /to-spec and /to-tickets, but that's not how it played out. This discrepancy makes sense because I had to do a big pivot from a client-specific wordpress CMS to a general wordpress CMS, which took more time with the grilling and rewriting the spec.\r\n    20\t* The 5 hour context percentage got to 54%, which was when I was doing the extra credit tickets. The plan was to use 3% per ticket. There were only 2 tickets, T15 and T16, and they spent 6% and 18% of the 5 hour window respectively, which is over the budget, but it added well to the project and adds a safety margin to the project grade with the extra credit.\r\n    21\t* The /code-review stage of the workflow chewed up a significant amount. At the point where I switched from Sonnet to Opus 5. High, as can be seen in the usage ledger, the 5 hour context percentage jumped up from 10% to 42%, because with my first run of Opus 5.5 High, I ran /code-review for the first time. The ticket T10 was very heavy on token usage in particular, since it resolved multiple bugs at once. T11 took 13% of the 5 hour context limit. These all show that I've gone over-budget from the originally planned idea, which was to get abotu 3% per ticket. To avoid this in the future, it's best to get Opus 5.5 High (or better, xHigh) running for the /implement phase as well, so that /code-review doesn't have such increased token usage. Also, to clarify, I ran /code-review after all the implementation tickets were complete, rather than running /code-review after every ticket as was expected.\r\n    22\t* Additionally, the extra credit tickets ended up filling a significant portion of both the context window and the 5 hour limit. The weekly limited was relatively untouched though. \r\n    23\t* This data shows me that the project required considerably more tokens that expected, and this is largely because of the pivot and the process of fixing bugs. Future budget plans should therefore include and take into account any potential unexpected bug fixing and project trajectory correction into the total token budget plan. Additionally, even though the more capable models chew up tokens more, they are certainly worth the extra tokens, because they notice many issues and fix those issues that other models don't pick up.\r\n    24\t\r\n====\nwarning: in the working copy of 'notes/cms-field-notes.md', LF will be replaced by CRLF the next time Git touches it\nwarning: in the working copy of 'notes/token-budget-plan.md', LF will be replaced by CRLF the next time Git touches it\n CONTEXT.md                                         |  4 +-\n README.md                                          | 69 ++++++++++++++--------\n ...400_mp2-web-cms_report_rajan-thakur_20261006.md | 11 ++--\n notes/cms-field-notes.md                           |  4 +-\n notes/token-budget-plan.md                         |  1 -\n notes/usage-ledger.csv                             | 15 +++++\n 6 files changed, 69 insertions(+), 35 deletions(-)\n2026-10-16T06:18:38Z,674d08af,revise,anthropic,Opus 5.5,xhigh,36.0,31,4\r\n2026-10-16T06:22:41Z,674d08af,revise,anthropic,Opus 5.5,xhigh,36.0,32,4\r\n2026-10-16T06:41:25Z,1055f71e,revise,anthropic,Opus 5.5,xhigh,17.0,40,5\r\n2026-10-16T07:04:45Z,1055f71e,revise,anthropic,Opus 5.5,xhigh,18.0,41,5\r\n2026-10-16T07:20:01Z,1055f71e,revise,anthropic,Opus 5.5,xhigh,18.0,42,6","is_error":false}]},"uuid":"11e63f03-3ef1-4bc6-80d7-174e1e8478c5","timestamp":"2026-10-16T07:24:08.568Z","toolUseResult":{"stdout":"     1\t# Project Report\r\n     2\t\r\n     3\t* (a) What I built and which grill decisions were mine  \r\n     4\tTo build the CMS I used the AI only, and none of the code for the CMS is mine.\r\n     5\tOne major grill decision I made were to pivot away from a client-specific CMS to a general CMS with a separate client website built using the CMS. This discrepancy makes sense because I had to do a big pivot from a client-specific wordpress CMS to a general wordpress CMS, which took more time with the grilling and rewriting the spec.\r"," * The 5 hour context percentage got to 54%, which was when I was doing the extra credit tickets. The plan was to use 3% per ticket. There were only 2 tickets, T15 and T16, and they spent 6% and 18% of the 5 hour window respectively, which is over the budget, but it added well to the project and adds a safety margin to the project grade with the extra credit.\r","-* The /code-review stage of the workflow chewed up a significant amount. At the point where I switched from Sonnet to Opus 5. High, as can be seen in the usage ledger, the 5 hour context percentage jumped up from 10% to 42%, because with my first run of Opus 5.5 High, I ran /code-review for the first time. The ticket T10 was very heavy on token usage in particular, since it resolved multiple bugs at once. T11 took 13% of the 5 hour context limit. These all show that I've gone over-budget from the originally planned idea, which was to get abotu 3% per ticket. To avoid this in the future, it's best to get Opus 5.5 High (or better, xHigh) running for the /implement phase as well, so that /code-review doesn't have such increased token usage. Also, to clarify, I ran /code-review after all the implementation tickets were complete, rather than running /code-review after every ticket as was expected.\r","+* The /code-review stage of the workflow chewed up a significant amount. At the point where I switched from Sonnet to Opus 5. High, as can be seen in the usage ledger, the 5 hour context percentage jumped up from 10% to 42%, because with my first run of Opus 5.5 High, I ran /code-review for the first time. The ticket T10 was very heavy on token usage in particular, since it resolved multiple bugs at once. T11 took 13% of the 5 hour context limit. These all show that I've gone over-budget from the originally planned idea, which was to get abotu 3% per ticket. To avoid this in the future, it's best to get Opus 5.5 High (or better, xHigh) running for the /implement phase as well, so that /code-review doesn't have such increased token usage. Also, to clarify, I ran /code-review after all the implementation tickets were complete, rather than running /code-review after every ticket as was originally expected.\r"," * Additionally, the extra credit tickets ended up filling a significant portion of both the context window and the 5 hour limit. The weekly limited was relatively untouched though. \r"," * This data shows me that the project required considerably more tokens that expected, and this is largely because of the pivot and the process of fixing bugs. Future budget plans should therefore include and take into account any potential unexpected bug fixing and project trajectory correction into the total token budget plan. Additionally, even though the more capable models chew up tokens more, they are certainly worth the extra tokens, because they notice many issues and fix those issues that other models don't pick up.\r"," "]}]}],"moreFiles":0,"changedFiles":["C:\\Rajan\\E disk\\My work\\IPHS400\\code\\mp2-cms\\README.md","C:\\Rajan\\E disk\\My work\\IPHS400\\code\\mp2-cms\\docs\\iphs400_mp2-web-cms_report_rajan-thakur_20261006.md"]}},"serverClassifierContext":{"request":"2d53e0fb-afb1-4d65-a264-7444ee127890","context":{"git_state":{"cwd":"/c/Rajan/E disk/My work/IPHS400/code/mp2-cms","root":"/c/Rajan/E disk/My work/IPHS400/code/mp2-cms","branch":"main","default_branch":null,"status":{"clean":false,"counts":{"staged":3,"modified":6,"untracked":null,"untracked_normal":3},"porcelain":null,"truncated":false},"visibility":{"origin":{"host":"github.com","remote":"Rajan-Thakur/iphs400-mp2-cms","visibility":"public"},"push_remote":"origin","remotes":[{"name":"origin","host":"github.com","remote":"Rajan-Thakur/iphs400-mp2-cms","visibility":"public"},{"name":"template","host":"github.com","remote":"jon-chun/iphs400-mp2-cms-starter","visibility":"unknown"}],"visibility_cache":[{"host":"github.com","remote":"Rajan-Thakur/iphs400-mp2-cms","visibility":"public"}]}},"live_cwd":"/c/Rajan/E disk/My work/IPHS400/code/mp2-cms","platform":"windows"}},"sourceToolAssistantUUID":"d87e0f78-4376-440a-844c-57503fa082d6","permissionDecision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reasonType":"classifier"},"session_id":"1055f71e-ccde-43ea-88c4-5fa4af27c26e","userType":"external","entrypoint":"cli","cwd":"C:\\Rajan\\E disk\\My work\\IPHS400\\code\\mp2-cms","sessionId":"1055f71e-ccde-43ea-88c4-5fa4af27c26e","version":"2.1.301","gitBranch":"main"}

{"parentUuid":"16d43af2-3344-4fda-a769-14f5865c8b02","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"36abf314-c0e6-4806-ba69-8607bcf6b5be","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_019VjTR58WjLrTTvzqGCjiNY","type":"tool_result","content":"# IPHS 400 — Mini-Project #2 (Web CMS)\n\n## Run it\n\n```bash\nuv sync\ncp .env.example .env\nuv run python scripts/seed_demo.py\nuv run cms serve        # then open http://localhost:8000/admin \n```\n\n## Run locally (run playwright install only once)\n...\n====\nOther grill decisions I made were generally refinements of what the AI proposed, such as what Admin/Editor permissions should look like (such as that Editors should be able to delete content, I decide\n\nWith that said, here's the comparison between the token budget plan and the usage ledger\n* The plan was to use about 20% on /grill-with-docs, /to-spec and /to-tickets, \n\nbut that's not how it played out. This discrepancy makes sense because I had to do a big pivot from a client-specific wordpress CMS to a general wordpress CMS, which took more time with the grilling and rewriting the spec.\n* The 5 hour context percentage got to 54%, which was when I was doing the extra credit tickets. The plan was to use 3% per ticket. There were only 2 tickets, T15 and T16, and they spent 6% and 18% of the 5 hour window respectively, which is over the budget, but it added well to the project and adds a safety margin to the project grade with the extra credit.\n* The /code-review stage of the workflow chewed up a significant amount. At the point where I switched from Sonnet to Opus 5. High, as can be seen in the usage ledger, the 5 hour context percentage went up from 10% to 42%, because with my first run of Opus 5.5 High, I ran /code-review for the first time. However, since the run is actually 5 days apart, the /code-review was run on a fresh 5 hour context, which means that 42% of the window was taken up by that /code-review run alone. The ticket T10 was very heavy on token usage in particular, since it resolved multiple bugs at once. T11 took 13% of the 5 hour context limit. These all show that I've gone over-budget from the originally planned idea, which was to get abotu 3% per ticket. To avoid this in the future, it's best to get Opus 5.5 High (or better, xHigh) running for the /implement phase as well, so that /code-review doesn't have such increased token usage.\n* Additionally, the extra credit tickets ended up filling a significant portion of both the context window and the 5 hour limit. The weekly limited was relatively untouched though. \n====\n.gitignore:2:*.db\tcms.db\ne9dfb18 Exercise B: usage_report.spend() sums meter increases across resets\nThe 5-hour and weekly meters reset to a lower value when their window\nrolls over, so spend() adds only the rise between consecutive readings,\nskipping blanks and treating any drop as a reset. This discrepancy makes sense because I had to do a big pivot from a client-specific wordpress CMS to a general wordpress CMS, which took more time with the grilling and rewriting the spec.\n* The 5 hour context percentage got to 54%, which was when I was doing the extra credit tickets. The plan was to use 3% per ticket. There were only 2 tickets, T15 and T16, and they spent 6% and 18% of the 5 hour window respectively, which is over the budget, but it added well to the project and adds a safety margin to the project grade with the extra credit.\n* The /code-review stage of the workflow chewed up a significant amount. At the point where I switched from Sonnet to Opus 5. High, as can be seen in the usage ledger, the 5 hour context percentage went up from 10% to 42%, because with my first run of Opus 5.5 High, I ran /code-review for the first time. However, since the run is actually 5 days apart, the /code-review was run on a fresh 5 hour context, which means that 42% of the window was taken up by that /code-review run alone. The ticket T10 was very heavy on token usage in particular, since it resolved multiple bugs at once. T11 took 13% of the 5 hour context limit. These all show that I've gone over-budget from the originally planned idea, which was to get abotu 3% per ticket. To avoid this in the future, it's best to get Opus 5.5 High (or better, xHigh) running for the /implement phase as well, so that /code-review doesn't have such increased token usage.\n* Additionally, the extra credit tickets ended up filling a significant portion of both the context window and the 5 hour limit. You could instead:\n- drop the counts from the report;\n- commit a screenshot of the Revisions list on the Contact Us edit screen;\n- or commit a CSV with only the revision rows (page, revision number, who saved it, when) and no user data. I can produce that from a copy of the database if you want.\n\n## Line 8: I was wrong, it's fine\nExercise B is the manual's graded exercise (Part 4): implementing `spend()` in `scripts/usage_report.py`, which adds up the 5-hour and weekly usage from the ledger. Stretch features **earn nothing in MP2**. MP2plus doesn't score a feature already present at `mp2plus-base`, so T15/T16 (revisions, scheduled publishing) are unscored everywhere. Don't merge template/main: it brings the instructor's ledger rows and sample transcripts.\n\n**Gap analysis 2026-10-16** (fresh clone at 2bcabc7: checker 22/22, 264 tests, judge-style walkthrough 59/59), estimated about 92/100.
